data.title: Service on partnerships other than limited partnerships
data.text:
(1) A commencement document may be served in the name of the partnership on every partnership other than a limited partnership that is the subject of a claim, (a) by being left (i) with an individual who is a partner, or (ii) with an individual who appears to have management or control responsibilities with respect to the partnership at its principal place of business or activity in Alberta, or at the partnership’s place of business or activity in Alberta where the claim arose, or (b) by being sent by recorded mail, addressed to the partnership, to the principal place of business or activity in Alberta of the partnership.
(2) Service is effected under subrule (1), (a) if the document is left with an individual in accordance with subrule (1)(a), on the date it is left, or (b) if the document is sent by recorded mail, on the date acknowledg- ment of receipt is signed.
(3) If a partner is a corporation, the commencement document may be served on that partner in accordance with rule 11.9(1) , and [Service on corporations] service on the partner is effected in accordance with rule 11.9(2).

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.11 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

data.title: Service on a corporation using another name
data.text:
(1) If a claim is made against a single corporation carrying on business or operating in a name other than its own, a commencement document may be served on that corporation (a) by being left (i) with an officer of the corporation who appears to have management or control responsibilities with respect to the corporation, or (ii) with an individual who appears to have management or control responsibilities with respect to the corporation at the principal place of business or activity in Alberta of the corporation, or at the place of business or activity in Alberta of the corporation at which the claim arose, or (b) by being sent by recorded mail, addressed to the business or operating name of the corporation, to the principal place of business or activity in Alberta of the corporation.
(2) Service is effected under this rule, (a) if the document is left with an individual in accordance with subrule (1)(a), on the date it is left, or (b) if the document is sent by recorded mail, on the date acknowledg- ment of receipt is signed.

data.title: Service on statutory and other entities
data.text:
(1) A commencement document may be served on an entity established by or under an enactment, or an entity not otherwise described in this Part, that is capable of being the subject of an action, (a) by being left (i) with an officer or administrator of the entity who appears to have management or control responsibilities with respect to the entity, or (ii) with an individual who appears to have management or control responsibilities with respect to the entity at the entity’s princi- pal place of business or activity in Alberta, or at the entity’s place of business or activity in Alberta where the claim arose, or (b) by being sent by recorded mail, addressed to the entity, to the entity’s principal place of business or activity in Alberta.
(2) Service is effected under this rule, (a) if the document is left with an individual in accordance with subrule (1)(a), on the date it is left, or (b) if the document is sent by recorded mail, on the date acknowledg- ment of receipt is signed.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.14 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

data.title: Service on person providing an address for service
data.text:
(1) In an action, a commencement document may be served on a person who has provided an address for service on a filed document (2) Service is effected under subrule (1), (a) if the document is left at the address, on the date it is left, or (b) if the document is sent by recorded mail, on the date acknowledg- ment of receipt is signed.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.15 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

(2) Service is effected under subrule (1)
(a) if the document is left at the address, on the date it is left, or
(b) if the document is sent by recorded mail, on the date acknowledg- ment of receipt is signed. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.15 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
After the commencement document is served, every party is required to signify an address at which it may be served with subsequent documents. The procedural rules provide or imply that the address for service can be changed from time to time as required. Service of process on the address for service is recognized as good service: rules 11.15, 11.17 and 11.22.18 As explained in Scarlett v. Sinclair, [2017] A.J. No. 1001, 2017 ABQB 582 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)). there are subtle but significant differences between service of commencement documents and non-commencement documents. Rule 11.5(2)(b) (dealing with service of commencement documents) requires acknowledgment of receipt by the individual to whom the document is addressed; rules 11.15(2) and 11.22(2) only require “acknowledgment of receipt”. (Rule 11.15 deals with serving commencement documents on someone who has provided an address for service; rule 11.22 deals with serving documents other than commencement documents by recorded mail.). Schlosser M. thought the looser requirements of rules 11.15 and 11.22 were “out of step with the methods of recorded mail” and possibly also “out of step with the overriding principle that the purpose of service is notice.” Scarlett v. Sinclair, [2017] A.J. No. 1001, 2017 ABQB 582 at para. 25 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)). He expressed the view that if he were called upon to decide the case on this point (the relevant issue before him being date of service of a statement of defence, a non-commencing document), he would be inclined to read in the wording of rule 11.5(2)(b) that the acknowledgment must be signed by the individual to whom service was addressed.
“...I have some difficulty”, he said, “finding that there is effective service if it was signed for by someone else and the addressee didn’t get it.”  Scarlett v. Sinclair, [2017] A.J. No. 1001, 2017 ABQB 582 at para. 25 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
The provision of an address for service by a plaintiff means service on that address is good service; the plaintiff cannot disavow service to this address if properly effected, Brace v. McKen, [2019] A.J. No. 452, 2019 ABCA 135 at para. 18 (Alta. C.A.). due to the effect of rules 11.2(c) and (d) in relation to non-commencement documents.
If a party fails to update their address for service, service on the former address for service can constitute good service. Espenilla v. Ayupan, [2019] A.J. No. 1692, 2019 ABCA 493 at para. 4 (Alta. C.A.).

data.title: Service on lawyer of record
data.text:
(1) A commencement document may be served on a party by being served on the lawyer of record for the party (a) by being left with the lawyer, being left at the lawyer’s office, or being left at another address specified by the lawyer, or (b) by being sent by recorded mail, addressed to the lawyer, to the lawyer’s office.
(2) Service is effected under this rule, (a) if the document is left with the lawyer or at the lawyer’s office or at another address specified by the lawyer, on the date it is left, or (b) if the document is sent by recorded mail, on the date acknowledg- ment of receipt is signed.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.17 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

(a) by being left with the lawyer, being left at the lawyer’s office, or being left at another address specified by the lawyer, or
(b) by being sent by recorded mail, addressed to the lawyer, to the lawyer’s office.
(2) Service is effected under this rule
(a) if the document is left with the lawyer or at the lawyer’s office or at another address specified by the lawyer, on the date it is left, or
(b) if the document is sent by recorded mail, on the date acknowledg- ment of receipt is signed. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.17 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
info_notes:
A lawyer of record is a lawyer whose name appears on a document filed in an action. For rules about lawyers of record, see Part 2 , [The Parties to Litigation] starting at rule 2.24 [Lawyer of record].
The lawyer may designate a document exchange facility as the lawyer’s address for service.

data.title: Service on business representatives of absent parties
data.text:
(1) A commence- ment document may be served on a party who is out of Alberta but who has a representative who resides and carries on the absent party’s business in Alberta, if the claim arose in respect of that business, (a) by being left with the representative, or (b) by being sent by recorded mail addressed to the representative.
(2) Service is effected under subrule (1), (a) if the document is left with the representative, on the date it is left, or (b) if the document is sent by recorded mail, on the date acknowledg- ment of receipt is signed by the representative.
(3) If the representative described in subrule (1) is a corporation, the corporation may be served in accordance with rule 11.9(1) [Service on corporations], and service is effected on the representative in accordance with rule 11.9(2).

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.19 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

hierarchy.heading: Division 3 – SERVICE OF DOCUMENTS, OTHER THAN COMMENCEMENT DOCUMENTS, IN ALBERTA

rules.title: Service of documents, other than commencement documents, in Alberta
rules.text:
Unless the Court otherwise orders or these rules or an enactment otherwise provides, every document, other than a commencement document, that is to be served in Alberta may only be served by (a) a method of service described in Division 2 [Service of Commence- ment Documents in Alberta] for service of a commencement document, [Recorded mail service]
(d) a method of service agreed to under rule 11.3 [Agreement between parties].

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.20 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
sentences: Unless the Court otherwise orders or these rules or an enactment otherwise provides, every document, other than a commencement document, that is to be served in Alberta may only be served by
(a) a method of service described in Division 2 [Service of Commence- ment Documents in Alberta] for service of a commencement document, [Recorded mail service]
(d) a method of service agreed to under rule 11.3 [Agreement between parties]. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.20 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
info_notes:
There are a few occasions when non-commencement documents must be served in the same way as commencement documents, for example • rule 9.21(3)(b) [Application for new judgment or order]
• rule 9.22(2)(c) [Application that judgment or order has been satisfied]
• rule 10.52(3)(a) .
[Declaration of civil contempt]
The methods of service described by rule 11.20(a) include service at an address for service on a filed document (under rule 11.15 [Service on a person providing an address for service]).
Either the original document or a copy of the original document may be served: see rule 11.1 .
[Service of original documents and copies]

commentary.text:
This division deals with service of documents that are not commence- ment documents. Care must be taken to properly identify the category of document required to be served.
Rule 11.20 provides that documents, other than commencement documents, can be served (1) by any methods applicable for service of the commencement document, (2) electronic, (3) recorded mail under rule 11.22, or (4) a method agreed by the parties. None of these methods provide for service by “regular mail,” although it might be permitted under a substitutional service order under rule 11.28.28

rules.title: Service by electronic method
rules.text:
(1) A document, other than a com- mencement document, may be served by electronic method on a person who has specifically provided an address to which information or data in respect of an action may be transmitted, if the document is sent to the person at the specified address, and (a) the electronic agent receiving the document at that address receives the document in a form that is usable for subsequent reference, and (b) the sending electronic agent obtains or receives a confirmation that the transmission to the address of the person to be served was successfully completed.
(2) Service is effected under subrule (1) when the sending electronic agent obtains or receives confirmation of the successfully completed transmission.
(3) In this rule, “ ” and “ ” have the same meanings electronic electronic agent as they have in the .
Electronic Transactions Act [Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.21 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz.August 14, 2010);Alta.
Reg. 163/2010, s. 8]

commentary.text:
Rule 11.21(1) allows a party to effect service of a non-commencement document by email if three conditions exist. “First, a party must ‘specifically provide ... an address to which information ... in respect of an action may be transmitted“. Second, the receiving party’s computer program must ‘receive ... the document in a form that is usable for subsequent reference’. Third, the sending party’s computer program must ‘obtain ... or ... receive a confirmation that the transmission to the address of the person to be served was successfully completed’.”29Simply stated, the communication must be both sent and received in a “usable” form for electronic service to be effective. Archer v. Ribbon Communications Canada ULC, [2019] A.J. No. 862, 2019 ABQB 481 at para. 16 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
Service is effected when the sender receives confirmation of successful transmission.  Covey v. Devon Canada Corp., [2020] A.J. No. 1352, 2020 ABCA 445 at para. 19 (Alta. C.A.).
A party who attempts to serve by email may be unable to prove the second or third elements of rule 11.21(1). Travis v. D & J Overhead Door Ltd., [2016] A.J. No. 1080, 2016 ABCA 319 at para. 147 (Alta. C.A.). One way to ensure this is so, is to request a read receipt from a recipient. If the strict requirements of this rule cannot be met, rule 11.27 could be used to nonetheless validate service.
Where a party includes an email address in the “Address for Service and Contact Information of Party Filing this Document” in documents filed with the court, they have objectively indicated that the party is prepared to receive service by email. Wang v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission), [2022] A.J. No. 153, 2022 ABQB 99 at para. 9 (Alta. Q.B.).
sentences: Rule 11.21(1) allows a party to effect service of a non-commencement document by email if three conditions exist. “First, a party must ‘specifically provide ... an address to which information ... in respect of an action may be transmitted“.
Second, the receiving party’s computer program must ‘receive ... the document in a form that is usable for subsequent reference’.

Third, the sending party’s computer program must ‘obtain ... or ... receive a confirmation that the transmission to the address of the person to be served was successfully completed’.”29Simply stated, the communication must be both sent and received in a “usable” form for electronic service to be effective.
Archer v. Ribbon Communications Canada ULC, [2019] A.J. No. 862, 2019 ABQB 481 at para. 16 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
Service is effected when the sender receives confirmation of successful transmission.
Covey v. Devon Canada Corp., [2020] A.J. No. 1352, 2020 ABCA 445 at para. 19 (Alta. C.A.).
A party who attempts to serve by email may be unable to prove the second or third elements of rule 11.21(1).
Travis v. D & J Overhead Door Ltd., [2016] A.J. No. 1080, 2016 ABCA 319 at para. 147 (Alta. C.A.).
One way to ensure this is so, is to request a read receipt from a recipient.

hierarchy.heading: Division 5 – SERVICE OF DOCUMENTS OUTSIDE ALBERTA

rules.title: Real and substantial connection
sentences: (1) A commencement document may be served outside Alberta and in Canada only if
(a) a real and substantial connection exists between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in the action is based, and
(2) A commencement document may be served outside Canada only if

(a) a real and substantial connection exists between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in an action is based and the commencement document is accompanied with a document or affidavit that sets out the grounds for service of the document outside Canada
(b) the Court, on application supported by an affidavit satisfactory to the Court, permits service outside Canada, and
(c) the person served with the commencement document is also served with a copy of the order permitting service outside Canada.

(3) Without limiting the circumstances in which a real and substantial connection may exist between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in an action is based, in the following circumstances a real and substantial connection is presumed to exist:
(a) the claim relates to land in Alberta
(b) the claim relates to a contract or alleged contract made, performed or breached in Alberta
(c) the claim is governed by the law of Alberta
(d) the claim relates to a tort committed in Alberta
(e) the claim relates to the enforcement of a security against property other than land by the sale, possession or recovery of the property in Alberta
(f) the claim relates to an injunction in which a person is to do or to refrain from doing something in Alberta
(g) the defendant is resident in Alberta
(h) the claim relates to the administration of an estate and the deceased died while ordinarily resident in Alberta
(i) the defendant, although outside Alberta, is a necessary or proper party to the action brought against another person who was served in Alberta
(j) the claim is brought against a trustee in relation to the carrying out of a trust in any of the following circumstances:
(i) the trust assets include immovable or movable property in Alberta and the relief claimed is only as to that property
(ii) the trustee is ordinarily resident in Alberta
(iii) the administration of the trust is principally carried on in R. 11.25 [Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.25 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz.August 14, 2010);Alta. Reg. 122/2012, s. 9]

commentary.text:
Whether an Alberta court assumes jurisdiction over an action involves two steps.37Rule 11.25 is concerned with the first step, which is whether there is jurisdiction simpliciter over the action, based on a real and substantial connection. If so, the action may be commenced in Alberta and served outside of Alberta. Second, because another forum outside of Alberta may also have jurisdiction based on a real and substantial simpliciter connection, it may be necessary to make a determination later on whether the court should choose to exercise jurisdiction as the most convenient forum, based on discretionary principles. Ayles v. Arsenault, [2011] A.J. No. 888, 2011 ABQB 493 at paras. 18-20 (Alta. Q.B.).
Rules 11.25(1) and (2) create significantly different approaches to service in Canada versus service outside of Canada. Rule 11.25(3) sets out circumstances in which a real and substantial connection is presumed to exist. Court v. Debaie, [2012] A.J. No. 1091, 2012 ABQB 640 at para. 8 (Alta. Q.B.).

rules.title: Validating service
rules.text:
(1) Except in respect of a document that must be served in accordance with Division 8 [Service in a Contracting State under the Hague Convention], the Court may, on application, make an order validating the service of a document served inside or outside Alberta in a manner that is not specified by these rules if the Court is satisfied that the method of service used brought or was likely to have brought the document to the attention of the person to be served.
(2) On application, the Court may make an order validating the service of a document served inside or outside Alberta if the Court is satisfied that the document would have been served on the person or would have come to the attention of the person if the person had not evaded service.
(3) If service is validated by the Court under this rule, service is effected on the date specified in the order.
(4) Subrules (1) and (3) apply despite any previous order that permitted or directed service of the document by a particular method.

rules.title: Substitutional service
rules.text:
(1) If service of a document, inside or outside Alberta, is impractical, the Court may, on application, make an order for substitutional service.
(2) The application must be supported by an affidavit (a) setting out why service is impractical, (b) proposing an alternative method of service, and (c) stating why the alternative method of service is likely to bring the document to the attention of the person to be served.
(3) Unless otherwise ordered, an order for substitutional service of a document must be served with the document except when substitutional service is by advertisement, in which case the advertisement must contain a reference to the order.
(4) If a document is served in accordance with an order for substitutional service, service is effected on the date specified in the order.

rules.title: Dispensing with service
rules.text:
(1) On application, the Court may make an order dispensing with service, inside or outside Alberta, if service of a document by a method prescribed by these rules is impractical or impossible.
(2) The application must be supported by an affidavit (a) setting out that all reasonable efforts to serve the document have been exhausted or are impractical or impossible, (b) stating why there is no or little likelihood that the issue will be disputed, and (c) stating that no other method of serving the document is or appears to be available.

commentary.text: Rule 11.29 “provides that the court may, on application supported by affidavit evidence, make an order dispensing with service if it is impractical or impossible.” These types of orders should be very rare and usually a last resort — or in the unusual case where lack of notice cannot be prejudicial. For example, it may be that no such order is required where it is an appellant who cannot be found to serve with the respondent’s documents, “or that a party cannot later complain of non-service where they failed to update their address for service on the Notice of Appeal.” R. v. Vazquez-Cabello, [2015] A.J. No. 691, 2015 ABCA 214 at para. 6 (Alta. C.A.). An order under rule 11.29 is available,

rules.title: Proving service of documents
rules.text:
(1) Service of a document in Alberta and service of documents other than commencement documents outside Alberta may be proved to have been effected (a) by an affidavit (i) stating that the person was served, (ii) describing the method of service, and grounds in , [2018] A.J. No. 864, 2018 ABCA 248 (Alta. C.A.); for additional authority R. v. Johannesson on this point, see also , [2021] A.J. No. 576, 2021 ABQB 339 at para. 12 (Alta.
Breitkreuz v. Breitkreuz Q.B.).
